newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine trade gap widens in Jan to $1.145 bln.
newsitem.headline: Philippine trade gap widens in Jan to $1.145 bln.

text.p: The Philippine monthly merchandise trade deficit widened to $1.145 billion in January from $816 million a year ago and $835 million in December last year, the National Statistics Office (NSO) said on Tuesday. Electronics and components accounted for the biggest import payments at $411.73 million, up by 43.8 percent from a year ago, the NSO said in a statement.
Telecommunications equipment and electrical machinery comprised the second largest import payment at $341.21 million.
In January, export receipts rose 19.2 percent to $1.692 billion. Import payments rose 26.9 percent to $2.837 billion.
The United States was the top source of imported goods for January, with total payments to that country accounting for $649.02 million, or 22.9 percent of the total.
Exports to the United States amounted to $581.68 million.
Japan, which accounted for 20.1 percent of the total imports, was the second largest source. Import payments totalled $569.11 million while exports were $282.76 million.
Ranked by broad categories, the import bill for capital goods totalled $1.040 billion in January, up 48 percent from a year ago.
Payments for raw materials and intermediate goods grew by 12.3 percent year-on-year to $1.173 billion.
Consumer goods and special transactions accounted for $307.66 million of the import payments in the month, or 10.8 percent of the total.
Economists said on Tuesday the latest trade deficit figure was not alarming, given widespread expectations that a gap would persist and that the balance of payments was in surplus.
"The country has always been a net importer," said Johnny Noe Ravelo, economist at Bankers Association of the Philippines. "The numbers are getting bigger because the economy is getting bigger."
Luz Lorenzo, economist at Peregrine Securities, said she had expected a higher import figure in January after "unusually low" import gains in November and December.
She expects the overall trade deficit in 1997 to come in at $15.3 billion compared with $11.79 billion in 1996. For the year, export growth should be around 25 percent, she said.
"This (monthly figure) is roughly in line," she said.
Rolando Valenzuela, a senior vice president at Philippine TA Securities, said a rise in imports led by purchases of capital goods would translate into higher productivity in the economy.
"If this is really capital expenditures, then I'm not really worried about it," he said.
He added, "We're still seeing positive balance of payments for 1997", estimating balance of payments to be a surplus of $2.7 billion this year from around $4 billion in 1996.
